title: Teach Me the Game You Played at Recess
subtitle: Trade a hand-clapping game or rhyme with a friend—and see what changes when a familiar bit of play moves between people.
imageAlt: Two friends seated across from each other at a kitchen table, trying a hand-clapping game with mismatched timing and amused expressions.
imageConcept: A close, lively view of two adult friends at a kitchen table attempting a hand-clapping rhyme together: one sets the rhythm while the other is half a beat behind, both smiling, with natural light and ordinary clothes rather than coordinated styling.
body: Start with the part you remember

One friend begins a hand-clapping game. The other watches, joins in, misses a beat, and asks to start again. Then a word comes out differently from the version she remembers—or the hands land in another pattern. That small stumble is not a problem to solve. It is the point of the exchange: a game can feel familiar to both people without being identical for either one.

Try it with a friend by trading games or rhymes you already know. No special equipment, rehearsal, or expert knowledge is needed; many traditional games ask little more than willing hands and a bit of room. The American Folklife Center’s collection includes hand-clapping games among the many forms of play people have documented [1]. Here, the aim is simpler than building an archive: spend time playing, notice what each person remembers, and let the differences remain visible.
Offer an invitation, not a test

Keep the opening easy: “Would you teach me a game or rhyme you remember from recess?” Your friend might have a hand-clapping pattern, a skipping rhyme, a guessing game, or only a fragment. You can offer one of your own in return. If neither person can recall a complete version, that is still enough to begin. A phrase, a gesture, or the way someone remembers choosing sides can open the conversation.

The Smithsonian’s guide gives a third-grader who knows hand-clapping games as an example of a tradition-bearer and offers guidelines for collecting folklife and oral history [2]. In practice, curiosity works better than a quiz. Ask what happens next, whether the rhythm speeds up, or what you do if somebody misses a clap. Leave space for “I’m not sure” and “that’s all I remember.” A conversation should make it easier to share, not require a perfect performance.

Ask your friend to teach the game at the pace that works for them. First listen to or watch one full round. Then break it into manageable pieces: the words, the hand pattern, and the moment when the sequence changes. Try each part slowly, then put them together. If the pattern involves touching hands, check that both of you are comfortable with the movement; adapt it or choose another game if not.

Make a second pass without stopping every time something goes wrong. The rhythm often makes more sense in motion than in explanation. If you lose the sequence, ask for the line or gesture just before the tricky moment. Then switch roles. The person who was teaching becomes the learner, and the first person demonstrates their own version. The Library of Congress notes that games can be passed from child to child, with later generations sometimes adding changes [3]. A variation is not automatically a mistake; it may be part of how the game has travelled.
Compare the versions without crowning a winner

After you have both tried the games, compare details rather than deciding which version is correct. Did the words match? Was the rhythm steady or quick? Did one person clap their own hands before reaching toward a partner? Did the game end with a challenge, a mistake, or a laugh? What part came back most clearly, and what part did you have to reconstruct together?

These questions are about each person’s memory, not a claim to represent everyone who played the game. Two friends may have learned different versions in the same schoolyard; one person may remember the words while another remembers the sequence of movements. That contrast can tell you something about how play gets carried between people. It cannot, by itself, settle where a game began or identify one definitive version. Let the conversation keep its proper scale: “This is how I remember it,” not “This is how everyone played.”
Ask about the route it took

Once the game is moving, you can ask where your friend remembers learning it. Maybe a sibling taught it, a classmate started it, or the memory is tied to a particular playground. Follow the route only as far as the person can—and wants to—go. Someone may remember a friend’s name but not the year; another may know the rhyme from home but have no idea who first brought it there.

 That makes “who taught you?” a useful opening, not a demand for a complete family tree. You might also ask whether the game was played in a particular place, whether older or younger children joined, or if the words changed when the group changed. Those details put the memory in context without turning your friend into a spokesperson for a whole school, neighborhood, or culture.
Let the people involved set the boundaries

A game can feel ordinary to one person and private, tender, or culturally specific to another. Check before asking for a recording or sharing a version outside the two of you. If you do record, agree first on what the recording is for, who will keep it, and whether it may be shown or posted. Permission to play is not automatically permission to publish. Either person can decline a question, stop the game, or decide that a particular rhyme stays in the room.

This is especially important if a game includes words, gestures, or a context that the person says should not be shared broadly. Do not pressure them to explain the boundary or treat a refusal as a mystery to investigate. The exchange remains worthwhile without documentation. A phone-free round may even make it easier to attend to timing, expression, and the way the two versions meet. If you keep notes afterward, write them for yourselves and ask before attaching someone’s name or story.
Keep the difference in the game

End by playing each version once more, this time with the details you have learned. Let the person teaching choose the pace; let the learner ask for a restart. You might discover a shared line that neither of you expected, or find that the versions have different endings. Neither outcome needs a verdict. The delight is partly in noticing how a small pattern has been remembered, carried, and reshaped—and how your own version may change after learning someone else’s.

Before you part, ask whether your friend would like to trade another game next time. Maybe you will each bring one, or maybe you will leave the invitation open. There is no need to turn the moment into a project, post, or proof of anyone’s cultural knowledge. Play it, listen to the story the other person chooses to tell, and let the game belong first to the people sharing it.
